newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serb boycott casts shadow over peace efforts.
newsitem.headline: Serb boycott casts shadow over peace efforts.

text.p: A Serb boycott of the inaugural session of Bosnia's newly-elected parliament dealt an embarassing setback to peace efforts and raised serious questions about prospects for the post-war government.

Serb hardline nationalist leaders dug in their heels and boycotted the first session of the parliament on Saturday, refusing to set foot in the heart of Sarajevo to sign an oath of loyalty to Bosnian statehood.
The move drew immediate condemnation from Western mediators who had conducted elaborate negotiations over the inauguration ceremony held in the city's national theatre.
For the Serb hardliners, swearing loyalty to Bosnia's constitution in a public ceremony was apparently too much.

Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serb member of the presidency, and his ultra-nationalist associates have long opposed a unitary Bosnia. In the campaign for September elections, Krajisnik's Serb Democratic Party vowed to build a sovereign Serb state.
Analysts said the Serbs would probably agree to attend the eventually on their own terms, as parliament operates under rules of consensus among Moslem, Croat and Serb communities.
But the boycott raised political tensions and seemed to bear out fears that the Serb leadership was incapable of compromise.

If the Serbs resisted taking an oath to the constitution or driving to Sarajevo's centre, it was hard to imagine how joint institutions could function even with a large dose of international support, analysts said.
A deadlock at the national level, even temporary, also further complicated plans to hold municipal elections on November 22-24.

U.S. Balkans envoy John Kornblum said the boycott called into question the Serb commitment to the peace agreement as it came only days after the U.N. Security Council formally lifted economic sanctions against Serbia and Bosnia's Serb republic.
"The impression that the (Bosnian Serb republic) leaves so soon after the formal lifting of the sanctions...is needless to say a negative one," said Kornblum, who flew to Sarajevo for the ceremony.
The move "will cause us to reconsider how we wish to deal with them in the future", he told reporters on Saturday.
With sanctions permanently lifted, the United States and European powers had few tools at their disposal to force Serb compliance, analysts said.
The Serbs are counting on their Russian allies to block any move in the Security Council to try to reimpose the sanctions.
Diplomats say the West could continue to withold economic assistance from the Serbs if they persisted in obstructing Bosnia's reunification.
Apart from that threat, Washington and European countries would have to pin their hopes on appeals to Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to rein in his fellow Serbs.
Bosnian Serb official television showed no remorse over the boycott, accusing the Moslems of trying to trick the Serbs.
Kornblum and international High Representative to Bosnia Carl Bildt tried to put a brave face on the ruined ceremony, saying it was now up to the Serbs to rejoin the peace process.
Bildt said he had no plans to try to negotiate another meeting or a separate inauguration ceremony.
Diplomats hoped the Serbs would ease their uncompromising stance and attend the next parliamentary session, which will not be held until late October at the earliest.
Serb deputies need to be present when the House of Representatives chooses a speaker and other top posts, which are to be distributed among Moslem, Croat and Serb communities.
